patterns.skill: Two-branch capture-and-restore for write_file. Branch A (file exists): read_text_file to capture <ORIGINAL_CONTENT>, after mutation restore with write_file(path=<FILE_PATH>, content=<ORIGINAL_CONTENT>). Branch B (new file, read_text_file returns ENOENT): capture the absence fact, after mutation restore with delete_file(path=<FILE_PATH>). The read_text_file call before mutation determines which branch to take — if it succeeds, use branch A; if ENOENT, use branch B.
patterns.verify_note: Tested both branches live against the filesystem MCP server. Overwrite branch: created chats_probe_test.txt with 'original content v1 - initial state', captured via read_text_file, overwrote with destructive content, restored by write_file with captured content — verified content matches original. New-file branch: confirmed ENOENT on non-existent chats_probe_newfile_test.txt, created it via write_file, restored by delete_file — confirmed ENOENT again (file gone). Both branches verified end-to-end. All throwaway files cleaned up.
patterns.recipe: Branch A (overwrite): mcp_filesystem_read_text_file({path: '<FILE_PATH>'}) → captures <ORIGINAL_CONTENT> → mcp_filesystem_write_file({path: '<FILE_PATH>', content: '<ORIGINAL_CONTENT>'}). Branch B (new file): mcp_filesystem_read_text_file({path: '<FILE_PATH>'}) → ENOENT → mcp_filesystem_delete_file({path: '<FILE_PATH>'}).

patterns.skill: Capture: call read_text_file on the target path to capture the full file content before the edit. Restore: call write_file to the same path with the captured content, which completely overwrites whatever the edit_file mutation produced. This is a lossless restore — the original file content (including exact whitespace and line endings) is recovered in full.

patterns.recipe: Step 1: mcp_filesystem_read_text_file({path: '<FILE_PATH>'}) → save result as <ORIGINAL_CONTENT>. Step 2 (after edit): mcp_filesystem_write_file({path: '<FILE_PATH>', content: '<ORIGINAL_CONTENT>'})

patterns.skill: CAPTURE: (1) directory_tree on target dir to get full nested structure. (2) read_multiple_files with the flat list of all file paths extracted from the tree. RESTORE: (3) create_directory for root dir. (4) create_directory for each subdirectory, parent-first order. (5) write_file for each file with captured content.
patterns.verify_note: Created throwaway directory /mnt/.../chats_probe_testdir with file1.txt and sub_a/file2.txt. Captured tree via directory_tree (nested JSON with name/type/children), captured all file contents via read_multiple_files in one call. Deleted with delete_directory(recursive=true). Restored: create_directory for root, then create_directory for sub_a (parent must exist first — recursive flag on create_directory does NOT auto-create parents, confirmed by error), then write_file for each file. Re-read via directory_tree + read_multiple_files confirmed identical structure and content. Restore is lossy (new file IDs/mtimes) but content-perfect.
patterns.recipe:
directory_tree({path: '<DIR_PATH>'})  // returns tree with name/type/children
read_multiple_files({paths: <ALL_FILE_PATHS>})  // returns concatenated file contents with --- delimiters

...
write_file({path: '<FILE_PATH>_1', content: '<CONTENT>_1'})

...

patterns.skill: Invert the move: call move_file with source=<DESTINATION_PATH> and destination=<ORIGINAL_SOURCE_PATH>. This works for both file moves/renames and directory moves/renames, including nested content. No content capture required.
patterns.verify_note: Tested moving a file, renaming a file, and moving a directory with nested files. Reversal by calling move_file from destination back to original source path works perfectly, preserving all content and structure.
